body: The square the whole district is divided into for scoring: 250 m a side, 6.25 hectares, 67,855 of them. Every figure on the map is one value for one of these. That is almost certainly larger than your field and in the wrong place, which is what drawing a plot fixes — the plot is scored from the cells it actually overlaps, weighted by how much of each it covers.

How well this ground matches what an enterprise needs, in the five classes of the FAO land evaluation framework. It is a statement about your land, not about the crop, and it says nothing about price or profit. The split that matters most is N1 against N2: N1 fails today on something work can fix, and the platform sizes that work. N2 fails on something nobody can change.

The requirement holding a score down hardest. Scores combine as a weighted geometric mean rather than an average, which is Liebig's law of the minimum: one badly wrong factor drags the whole result down, because a farmer cannot eat the average of good rainfall and impossible soil. The panels list requirements worst-first for the same reason.

How much of a score actually had data behind it, as a percentage of the weighted requirements. Where a reading is missing it is left out rather than assumed satisfied, so the coverage figure falls and the panel says so. A score of 70 on 60% coverage and a score of 70 on full coverage are not the same claim.

Three different things, labelled wherever they appear. Measured is read from a satellite or a soil survey. Modelled is computed from something that was measured — pond temperature from air temperature, erosion exposure from rain, soil and slope. Inferred is a stand-in for something nobody measured here at all, like peat depth from soil carbon. Anything not measured carries a note saying so.

A projected future climate rather than a forecast. SSP2-4.5 is the middle-of-the-road emissions pathway and SSP5-8.5 the high one; the picker offers 2030, 2050 and 2070 under each. Choosing one re-scores everything against that climate. It matters most for long commitments: a rubber or oil palm stand planted now spends most of its life in a climate nobody has farmed yet.

Every projected figure here is the middle of six climate models that disagree with each other. The spread — the tenth and ninetieth percentiles — is shown beside it, and it is wide. A projection given without its spread reads as a measurement, which it is not.
The thirty-year average that counts as "today" here. Typical conditions over a period long enough that one odd year does not move it, and the reference every projected change is measured against.

The botanical group a crop belongs to, and the unit the rotation rules work in. Bacterial wilt does not distinguish tomato from chilli, so as far as the soil is concerned planting one after the other is planting the same crop twice. Some pests cross families too, which is why a few rules name specific crops instead.

A plant that takes nitrogen out of the air and leaves some of it in the soil for whatever follows. Groundnut, soybean, long bean, and the two green manures. How much is left behind differs: a grain legume exports most of its nitrogen in the seed, while a green manure turned in whole keeps all of it.

A crop grown to be cut and turned into the soil rather than harvested. It costs a season's income and pays it back in nitrogen, organic matter and a break in the pest cycle. Only the build-the-soil rotation strategy will ever propose one, because it is the only one that scores what a season leaves behind as well as what it takes off.

What is left on the field after harvest — stubble, haulm, leaf. It is where soil organic carbon comes from, and crops are rated high, medium or low on how much of it they leave. Maize leaves a lot; a short-cycle leaf vegetable leaves almost nothing.

How green a patch of ground is, measured from space. Living leaves reflect near-infrared light strongly and absorb red light, so the gap between the two bands tracks how much leaf is there; NDVI puts that gap on a scale where bare soil is near zero and closed tropical canopy is above 0.8. It measures leaf, not yield and not health: a weed-covered field and a good crop can read the same. Here it comes from MODIS at 250 m, which is the one dataset in this platform at the same resolution as the analysis cell, averaged over three complete years. Cloud is the limit — each figure is built from the 16-day composites that got a clear look, and where too few did, the cell is left blank rather than guessed.

The difference between the greenest and the barest month of an average year. It is the more useful of the two greenness figures: the mean mostly tells you this is Borneo, while the swing separates ground that is green all year — rubber, oil palm, forest — from ground that goes bare and back, which is what an annual crop looks like from orbit. That rhythm is the one a new rotation has to fit into. Neither figure counts towards any suitability score, deliberately: greenness records what is growing now, so scoring it would recommend land because something else already has it.

What an enterprise asks of a household, each on a scale of one to five: how much work it takes through the season, and how much money it needs before the first harvest. Chilli and tomato are the hardest work in this catalogue; beef cattle needs the most capital; a green manure asks for almost neither. Both are shown on an enterprise's own panel and neither counts towards its score, because how much work a crop is says nothing about whether this ground suits it.

Not in this platform at all. There is no price series, no market data and no gross margin anywhere in it, so nothing it recommends has been weighed against what you would be paid for it — which is why there are six priority sliders and none of them is about money. The two economic figures it does hold are what an enterprise asks in labour and capital, which are shown rather than scored, and what a piece of remedial work would cost, which is real ringgit at catalogue rates. Everything else about the economics of a decision is yours and your buyer's.

The materials and volumes a sized design would need, with an indicative cost at catalogue rates. Every design also lists what it rests on — which figure came from where, and which inputs are assumptions. It is written to be taken to a contractor and argued with, not to be ordered from.

How far soil moisture has departed from normal for the time of year — the standard way of saying a field is drier than it should be in May. This platform does not compute it. It needs an observed soil moisture record, which would come from NASA SMAP, and SMAP is registered in the data catalogue and has never been ingested. What the platform has instead is a modelled water balance: rainfall minus what a crop loses to the air, month by month. That is a different thing, and it is not checked against any observation.
